###

###

###

###

text:
The wealthy and reclusive Mr. Edward Blackstone had been found dead in his mansion, a grand estate nestled in the English countryside. The local police were baffled by the lack of evidence and the seemingly impossible nature of the crime. As Detective Jameson began to investigate, he learned that Mr. Blackstone had been hosting a small dinner party on the night of his murder, with a guest list that included his business partner, Mrs. White; his personal assistant, Mr. Jenkins; his nephew, Mr. Thomas Brown; and a mysterious stranger, Mr. Lucas Ross, who had been invited at the last minute. The guests had all reported hearing nothing unusual on the night of the murder, but Detective Jameson noticed that Mr. Ross seemed particularly nervous and agitated during the initial questioning.

###

As the detective continued to question the guests, he discovered that Mr. Blackstone had been acting strangely in the days leading up to his death, often arguing with Mrs. White over business matters and seeming increasingly paranoid. Mrs. White, a tall, imposing figure with a sharp tongue, had been openly hostile towards Mr. Blackstone during the dinner party, and the other guests had witnessed several heated exchanges between them. Mr. Jenkins, on the other hand, had been his usual quiet and reserved self, taking notes and pouring drinks with his customary efficiency. Mr. Thomas Brown had been chatting amiably with Mr. Ross, discussing everything from politics to literature, and had seemed to be getting along famously with the mysterious stranger. But it was Mrs. White's animosity towards the victim that caught the detective's attention, and he made a mental note to look into her alibi for the time of the murder.

###

Detective Jameson's conversation with Mr. Ross revealed that the stranger had been invited to the dinner party by Mr. Blackstone himself, who had apparently met him at a charity gala a few weeks prior. Mr. Ross seemed evasive when asked about the details of their conversation, claiming that they had only discussed trivial matters, but the detective sensed that there was more to the story. Mr. Ross also mentioned that he had stepped outside for some fresh air during the dinner party, and had been gone for about 20 minutes, during which time he claimed to have taken a walk around the gardens. When asked if anyone could confirm his alibi, Mr. Ross hesitated before saying that he had run into Mr. Jenkins, who was taking out the trash, and had exchanged a brief word with him. The detective made a note to speak with Mr. Jenkins again, to verify Mr. Ross's story, and to ask him more about his own whereabouts during the time of the murder. Meanwhile, Mrs. White was overheard arguing with Mr. Thomas Brown in the corner of the room, their voices hushed but their body language tense.

###

As the detective continued his investigation, he began to uncover some interesting details about the relationships between the guests. It seemed that Mr. Thomas Brown had been in deep financial trouble, and had been relying on his uncle, Mr. Blackstone, for support. However, Mr. Blackstone had recently informed his nephew that he would be cutting him off, citing his reckless spending habits and lack of responsibility. This had apparently led to a significant rift between the two, with Mr. Thomas Brown storming out of the house on several occasions. Mrs. White, on the other hand, seemed to have a solid alibi for the time of the murder, as several of the staff members reported seeing her in the kitchen, helping with the dessert course. Mr. Jenkins, as usual, was quiet and unassuming, but the detective noticed that he seemed to be watching Mr. Ross with a keen eye, as if sizing him up. Meanwhile, Mr. Ross himself was pacing back and forth in the library, muttering to himself and glancing at his watch for what felt like the hundredth time.

###

The detective's attention was drawn to a small, almost imperceptible tremble in Mr. Ross's hand as he lit a cigarette, and he couldn't help but wonder what was causing the man's evident agitation. As he watched, Mr. Ross glanced around the room, his eyes lingering on the other guests before finally coming to rest on Mrs. White, who was still arguing with Mr. Thomas Brown in hushed tones. The detective followed Mr. Ross's gaze, and noticed that Mrs. White's face was red with anger, her eyes flashing with a fierce intensity. For a moment, it seemed as though she might lash out at her companion, but then she appeared to regain control of herself, and the argument seemed to dissipate. The detective made a mental note to look into Mrs. White's background, to see if there were any other instances of her temper getting the better of her. As he did so, he noticed a small piece of paper on the floor, partially hidden under the couch cushion. He walked over to pick it up, and found that it was a receipt from a local hardware store, with a handwritten note on the back that read "Meet me at the old oak at midnight". The receipt was dated the night before the murder.

###

The detective's eyes scanned the room, trying to determine who might have written the note and who the intended recipient might have been. Mr. Ross was still pacing back and forth, his eyes fixed on the floor, while Mrs. White and Mr. Thomas Brown had moved on to a new topic of conversation, their argument apparently forgotten. Mr. Jenkins, however, seemed to have noticed the detective's discovery, and his eyes flicked briefly to the receipt before returning to his usual neutral expression. The detective tucked the receipt into his pocket, making a mental note to investigate further. He then turned his attention to Mr. Ross, who was now standing by the window, staring out into the garden. "Mr. Ross," the detective said, his voice firm but polite, "can you tell me where you were at midnight last night?" Mr. Ross turned, his eyes widening slightly as he replied, "I was in my room, asleep. I didn't leave until I came downstairs for breakfast this morning." The detective raised an eyebrow, intrigued by the faint hesitation in Mr. Ross's voice.

###

The detective's eyes narrowed slightly as he pressed Mr. Ross for more information. "Can anyone confirm that you were in your room at midnight?" he asked, his tone neutral. Mr. Ross hesitated, his eyes darting to the side before returning to the detective. "I don't think so," he said finally. "I was alone in my room. But I'm sure I didn't leave the house. I wouldn't have had any reason to." The detective nodded thoughtfully, making a note on his pad. He then turned to the other guests, asking if anyone had seen or heard anything unusual around midnight. Mrs. White and Mr. Thomas Brown both shook their heads, but Mr. Jenkins spoke up, his voice low and measured. "I did hear something," he said. "I was walking past Mr. Ross's room on my way to get a glass of water, and I thought I heard a noise coming from inside. It sounded like someone was getting dressed." The detective's eyes snapped back to Mr. Ross, who was now frowning, his eyes clouded with concern.

###

The detective's gaze lingered on Mr. Ross, searching for any sign of deception, but the man's expression seemed genuinely puzzled. "What time was this, Mr. Jenkins?" the detective asked, his eyes still fixed on Mr. Ross. Mr. Jenkins thought for a moment before responding, "I'd say it was around 12:15. I remember checking the clock in the hallway before I went to get my water." The detective nodded, his mind racing with the implications. If Mr. Jenkins was telling the truth, it meant that Mr. Ross could have potentially slipped out of the house around midnight, despite his earlier denial. The detective made a note to investigate Mr. Ross's alibi further, and to ask the staff if they had seen or heard anything unusual around that time. As he did so, he noticed Mrs. White watching him with an intense gaze, her eyes seeming to bore into his skin. For a moment, he wondered if she might be trying to distract him from something, but then she looked away, her expression smoothing out into its usual calm mask.

###

As the investigation continued, the detective began to focus more closely on Mr. Ross, asking him a series of probing questions about his activities on the night of the murder. Mr. Ross seemed to be growing increasingly agitated, his responses becoming more and more defensive. The detective noticed that Mrs. White was watching the exchange with great interest, her eyes flicking back and forth between Mr. Ross and the detective. At one point, she even leaned forward, as if she were about to intervene, but then seemed to think better of it and sat back in her chair. Mr. Thomas Brown, on the other hand, seemed entirely uninterested in the proceedings, lounging in his chair with a look of bored indifference. Mr. Jenkins, however, was watching the scene with a keen eye, his expression thoughtful and observant. The detective wondered what might be going through his mind, and made a mental note to speak with him again later. Just then, one of the maids knocked at the door, and the detective excused himself to speak with her. ###

The maid, a timid-looking young woman named Emily, spoke to the detective in hushed tones, her eyes darting nervously around the hallway. "I didn't want to say anything in front of the others, sir," she said, "but I saw something last night that might be important. I was walking past Mr. Ross's room, and I saw him arguing with...with someone." The detective's ears pricked up, and he leaned in closer to the maid. "Who was he arguing with?" he asked, his voice low and urgent. Emily hesitated, glancing around the hallway again before responding. "It was Mrs. White, sir. The detective's eyes widened in surprise, and he made a mental note to look into Mrs. White's alibi again. He had been so focused on Mr. Ross as the potential suspect, but now it seemed that Mrs. White might be more involved than he had initially thought. As he thanked Emily and sent her back to her duties, he couldn't help but wonder what Mrs. White and Mr. Ross might have been arguing about, and whether it might have had something to do with the murder.

###

As he entered the room, Mrs. White looked up at him, a calm and composed expression on her face. "Yes, Detective?" she asked, her voice smooth and unruffled. The detective pulled up a chair and sat down beside her, his eyes locked on hers. "I've just received some information that suggests you and Mr. Ross had an argument last night," he said, his voice firm but polite. "Can you tell me what that was about?" Mrs. White's expression didn't change, but the detective noticed a faint flicker in her eyes, a brief moment of unease before she regained her composure. "Oh, that," she said, waving her hand dismissively. "It was just a silly disagreement about nothing important. I'm surprised anyone even noticed." The detective raised an eyebrow, skeptical of her response. He pressed her for more information, but she insisted that it was just a trivial matter, and not worth discussing further. As he continued to question her, he couldn't shake the feeling that she was hiding something, and that the argument with Mr. Ross might be more significant than she was letting on.

###

"I think I can clarify what happened, Detective," he said, his eyes locked on Mrs. White. "We were discussing a business matter, and we had a difference of opinion. Instead, she sat back in her chair, her expression icy and controlled. The detective's eyes narrowed, sensing that there was more to the story than either Mrs. White or Mr. Ross was letting on. He made a note to look into their business dealings, to see if there was any connection between their argument and the murder. As he did so, he noticed Mr. Thomas Brown watching the exchange with a curious expression, his eyes darting back and forth between Mrs. White and Mr. Ross. The detective wondered if Mr. Brown might know more than he was letting on, and made a mental note to speak with him again later. Meanwhile, Mr. Jenkins sat quietly, observing the scene with an intent gaze, his eyes seeming to bore into the very souls of the people around him.
